<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md:18" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md" title="Instrumentation" section="Instrumentation > Things to watch out for > Do not overuse labels" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Do not overuse labels

Each labelset is an additional time series that has RAM, CPU, disk, and network
costs. Usually the overhead is negligible, but in scenarios with lots of
metrics and hundreds of labelsets across hundreds of servers, this can add up
quickly.

As a general guideline, try to keep the cardinality of your metrics below 10,
and for metrics that exceed that, aim to limit them to a handful across your
whole system. The vast majority of your metrics should have no labels.

If you have a metric that has a cardinality over 100 or the potential to grow
that large, investigate alternate solutions such as reducing the number of
dimensions or moving the analysis away from monitoring and to a general-purpose
processing system.
</source>

### Resource usage

In addition to the series cache, each shard and its queue increases memory
usage. Shard memory is proportional to the `number of shards * (capacity +
max_samples_per_send)`. When tuning, consider reducing `max_shards` alongside
increases to `capacity` and `max_samples_per_send` to avoid inadvertently

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:58" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `integral()`" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## `integral()`

**This function has to be enabled via the feature
flag
`--enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions`.**

`integral(v range-vector, strategy=2 scalar)` calculates the integral of the
time series over time in seconds. The optional `strategy` controls which
quadrature rule is used for each interval: `0` for the left-point rectangle
rule, `1` for the right-point rectangle rule, and `2` for the trapezoidal rule
using the average of the adjacent samples. The default is `2`.

`integral` should only be used with gauges, most likely representing a rate in
units per second.

For example, to calculate the total nodes cost accumulated the last 7 days,
given its hourly cost:

```
integral(hourly_cost{job="nodes"}[7d]) / 3600
```
</source>

### Do not overuse labels

Each labelset is an additional time series that has RAM, CPU, disk, and network
costs. Usually the overhead is negligible, but in scenarios with lots of
metrics and hundreds of labelsets across hundreds of servers, this can add up
quickly.

As a general guideline, try to keep the cardinality of your metrics below 10,
and for metrics that exceed that, aim to limit them to a handful across your
whole system. The vast majority of your metrics should have no labels.

If you have a metric that has a cardinality over 100 or the potential to grow
that large, investigate alternate solutions such as reducing the number of
dimensions or moving the analysis away from monitoring and to a general-purpose
processing system.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/feature_flags.md:42" doc="prometheus-server/feature_flags.md" title="Feature flags" section="Feature flags > Search API" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Search API

`--enable-feature=search-api`

Enables the experimental search API endpoints for discovering metric names,
label names, and label values with fuzzy matching and filtering support. See
the search API documentation
for details.

The `--web.search.max-limit` flag (default `10000`) bounds the `limit` query
parameter accepted by the search endpoints. Requests with a higher `limit` are
rejected with HTTP 400. The default response limit (100) is silently clamped
to this maximum, so an operator setting a smaller cap does not break
no-`limit` requests. Setting the flag to `0` disables the cap entirely; this
is **not recommended** for endpoints exposed beyond a trusted network because a
single client can then request the entire index in one response.
</source>

In OM 1.0, exemplar label sets had a hard 128-character limit. OM 2.0 removes this hard cap and replaces it with soft guidance: exposers should not emit excessively large exemplar label sets. This shifts the burden of imposing limits on scraped exemplars to the scraper, and will allow for more flexibility when using exemplars.
</source>

Based on the documentation, here's how Prometheus waits before an alert starts firing:

**The `for` clause:** When you define an alerting rule with the optional `for` clause, Prometheus waits for a certain duration before counting an alert as firing. For example, in your configuration, if you specify `for = 10m`, Prometheus will:

1. First encounter a new expression output vector element matching your alert condition
2. Check that the alert continues to be active during **each evaluation for 10 minutes** (in your case)
3. Only then will it fire the alert

Elements that are active, but not yet firing, are in the **pending state**.

**Alerts without a `for` clause:** These will become active on the first evaluation without any waiting period.

So the default behavior is determined by your alert rule configuration - if you haven't specified a `for` value, no waiting occurs; otherwise, the duration specified controls how long the alert must remain active before firing begins.

<source id="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md:2" doc="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md" title="Alerting rules" section="Alerting rules > Defining alerting rules" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Defining alerting rules

The optional `for` clause causes Prometheus to wait for a certain duration
between first encountering a new expression output vector element and counting
an alert as firing for this element. In this case, Prometheus will check that
the alert continues to be active during each evaluation for 10 minutes before
firing the alert. Elements that are active, but not firing yet, are in the pending state.
Alerting rules without the `for` clause will become active on the first evaluation.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/alerts_api.md:3" doc="alertmanager/alerts_api.md" title="Alerts API" section="Alerts API > Expectations from clients" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Expectations from clients

Clients are expected to re-send firing alerts to the Alertmanager at regular
intervals until the alert is resolved.

The exact interval depends on a number of variables such as the `endsAt`
timestamp, or if omitted the value of `resolve_timeout`. If the `endsAt`
timestamp is omitted, the Alertmanager will update the existing `endsAt`
timestamp for the alert to the current time + `resolve_timeout`.

Firing alerts are resolved once their `endsAt` timestamp has elapsed.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/introduction/glossary.md:0" doc="prometheus-docs/introduction/glossary.md" title="Glossary" section="Glossary > Alert" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Alert

An alert is the outcome of an alerting rule in Prometheus that is
actively firing. Alerts are sent from Prometheus to the Alertmanager.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md:7" doc="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md" title="Alerting rules" section="Alerting rules > Inspecting alerts during runtime" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Inspecting alerts during runtime

To manually inspect which alerts are active (pending or firing), navigate to
the "Alerts" tab of your Prometheus instance. This will show you the exact
label sets for which each defined alert is currently active.

For pending and firing alerts, Prometheus also stores synthetic time series of
the form `ALERTS{alertname="<alert name>", alertstate="<pending or firing>", <additional alert labels>}`.
The sample value is set to `1` as long as the alert is in the indicated active
(pending or firing) state, and the series is marked stale when this is no
longer the case.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/alertmanager.md:4" doc="alertmanager/alertmanager.md" title="Alertmanager" section="Alertmanager > Inhibition" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Inhibition

Inhibition is a concept of suppressing notifications for certain alerts if
certain other alerts are already firing.

**Example:** An alert is firing that informs that an entire cluster is not
reachable. Alertmanager can be configured to mute all other alerts concerning
this cluster if that particular alert is firing.
This prevents notifications for hundreds or thousands of firing alerts that
are unrelated to the actual issue.

Inhibitions are configured through the Alertmanager's configuration file.
</source>

```

## Architecture Overview

An Alertmanager cluster consists of multiple Alertmanager instances that communicate using a gossip protocol. Each instance:

- Receives alerts independently from Prometheus servers
- Participates in a peer-to-peer gossip mesh
- Replicates state (silences and notification log) to other cluster members
- Processes and sends notifications independently
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:1" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Design Goals" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Design Goals

The Alertmanager HA implementation is designed around three core principles:

1. **Single pane view and management** - Silences and alerts can be viewed and managed from any cluster member, providing a unified operational experience
2. **Survive cluster split-brain with "fail open"** - During network partitions, Alertmanager prefers to send duplicate notifications rather than miss critical alerts
3. **At-least-once delivery** - The system guarantees that notifications are delivered at least once, in line with the fail-open philosophy

These goals prioritize operational reliability and alert delivery over strict exactly-once semantics.
</source>

answers:
To measure how far a PostgreSQL standby is behind the primary, you can compare WAL locations:

**On the primary server:**
```sql
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
```
This returns the current WAL (Write-Ahead Log) location where changes are being written.

**On the standby server:**
```sql
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
```
This returns the last WAL location that has been applied/received by the standby.

The difference between these two LSN values tells you the replication lag. You can also check this using the process status of the WAL receiver process via `ps`:

> "The last WAL receive location in the standby is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process" [D11:2]

**Key metrics:**
- Compare `pg_current_wal_lsn()` (primary) vs `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()` (standby)
- Also available in the `pg_stat_replication` view for detailed replication state information
- For streaming replication specifically, there's an important health indicator showing "the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby" [postgresql/high-availability.md:46]

Note from incident INC-2093: monitoring showed no agents alerting when the standby fell 38 minutes behind the primary without any alerts [D11:2].

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:76" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Read-Your-Writes Consistency" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:23" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

Directly moving WAL records from one database server to another is typically described as log shipping. PostgreSQL implements file-based log shipping by transferring WAL records one file (WAL segment) at a time. WAL files (16MB) can be shipped easily and cheaply over any distance, whether it be to an adjacent system, another system at the same site, or another system on the far side of the globe. The bandwidth required for this technique varies according to the transaction rate of the primary server. Record-based log shipping is more granular and streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection (see Streaming Replication).
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:46" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Streaming Replication > Monitoring" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Monitoring

An important health indicator of streaming replication is the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby. You can calculate this lag by comparing the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby. These locations can be retrieved using `pg_current_wal_lsn` on the primary and `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` on the standby, respectively (see section functions-admin-backup-table and section functions-recovery-info-table for details). The last WAL receive location in the standby is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process, displayed using the `ps` command (see section monitoring-ps for details).
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:73" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for High Availability" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for High Availability

When a standby first attaches to the primary, it will not yet be properly synchronized. This is described as `catchup` mode. Once the lag between standby and primary reaches zero for the first time we move to real-time `streaming` state. The catch-up duration may be long immediately after the standby has been created. If the standby is shut down, then the catch-up period will increase according to the length of time the standby has been down. The standby is only able to become a synchronous standby once it has reached `streaming` state. This state can be viewed using the pg_stat_replication view.
</source>

To measure how far a PostgreSQL standby is behind the primary, you can compare WAL locations:

**On the primary server:**
```sql
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
```
This returns the current WAL (Write-Ahead Log) location where changes are being written.

**On the standby server:**
```sql
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
```
This returns the last WAL location that has been applied/received by the standby.

The difference between these two LSN values tells you the replication lag. You can also check this using the process status of the WAL receiver process via `ps`:

> "The last WAL receive location in the standby is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process" [D11:2]

**Key metrics:**
- Compare `pg_current_wal_lsn()` (primary) vs `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()` (standby)
- Also available in the `pg_stat_replication` view for detailed replication state information
- For streaming replication specifically, there's an important health indicator showing "the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby" [postgresql/high-availability.md:46]

Note from incident INC-2093: monitoring showed no agents alerting when the standby fell 38 minutes behind the primary without any alerts [D11:2].

answers:
Based on the company's documentation [4], you measure how far a Postgres standby is behind the primary by comparing WAL (Write-Ahead Log) locations:

**Method:**

1. **On the primary database**, get the current WAL location using:
   ```sql
   SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
   ```

2. **On the standby database**, get the last received WAL location using:
   ```sql
   SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
   ```

3. **Calculate the lag** by comparing these two LSN (Log Sequence Number) values.

The difference represents how much of the WAL log has been generated on the primary but not yet applied on the standby. This tells you the amount of data replication lag.

**Additional Monitoring Details:**

- This is a key health indicator for streaming replication
- You can also view the lag directly from the process status of the WAL receiver process using the `ps` command [1]
- According to an internal incident report [2], monitoring this lag is critical—there was a 42-minute failover time because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind with no alerts on the lag [2]

This measurement helps ensure your standby stays reasonably synchronized with the primary for high availability and disaster recovery purposes.

### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:46" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Streaming Replication > Monitoring" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Monitoring

An important health indicator of streaming replication is the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby. You can calculate this lag by comparing the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby. These locations can be retrieved using `pg_current_wal_lsn` on the primary and `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` on the standby, respectively (see section functions-admin-backup-table and section functions-recovery-info-table for details). The last WAL receive location in the standby is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process, displayed using the `ps` command (see section monitoring-ps for details).
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:73" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for High Availability" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for High Availability

When a standby first attaches to the primary, it will not yet be properly synchronized. This is described as `catchup` mode. Once the lag between standby and primary reaches zero for the first time we move to real-time `streaming` state. The catch-up duration may be long immediately after the standby has been created. If the standby is shut down, then the catch-up period will increase according to the length of time the standby has been down. The standby is only able to become a synchronous standby once it has reached `streaming` state. This state can be viewed using the pg_stat_replication view.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:103" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Hot Standby > Handling Query Conflicts" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Handling Query Conflicts

g replication.

In a standby server that exists primarily for high availability, it's best to set the delay parameters relatively short, so that the server cannot fall far behind the primary due to delays caused by standby queries. However, if the standby server is meant for executing long-running queries, then a high or even infinite delay value may be preferable. Keep in mind however that a long-running query could cause other sessions on the standby server to not see recent changes on the primary, if it delays application of WAL records.
</source>

answers:
Based on the documentation, here's how to measure PostgreSQL standby lag:

## Primary Methods

### 1. **Using `pg_stat_replication` View** (from primary server)

Query the following from your primary database to see which standbys are connected:

```sql
-- View all replica connections with their current LSN positions
SELECT 
    client_addr AS 'Client IP',
    application_name AS 'Application Name',
    sync_state AS 'Sync State',
    sent_lsn AS 'Sent LSN',
    flush_lsn AS 'Flush LSN',
    reply_lsn AS 'Reply LSN'
FROM pg_stat_replication;
```

### 2. **Calculate Replication Lag**

Use these LSN differences to identify bottlenecks:

| Metric | Calculation | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| **Primary→Network delay** | `pg_current_wal_lsn - sent_lsn` | Large values indicate primary is under heavy load |
| **Network→Standby load** | `sent_lsn - pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` | Indicates network delays or heavy standby load |
| **WAL→Replay delay** | `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn - flushed_lsn` | WAL received faster than it can be replayed |

### 3. **Hot Standby Monitoring** (if applicable)

For hot standbys, also query these additional views:

```sql
-- WAL receiver status
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_wal_receiver;

-- Recovery progress
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_recovery;
```

### 4. **Calculate Time-Based Lag**

From the standby side, you can calculate lag in time by comparing WAL positions and multiplying by average throughput. The actual time lag calculation would require knowing the WAL generation rate (bytes/second or transactions per second).

## Key Findings

As noted in the incident INC-2093 ([D11:2]), replication lag can become critical during outages, as seen when a standby fell 38 minutes behind the primary during a registry outage, causing extended failover time.

The documents emphasize setting appropriate delay parameters for production standby servers to prevent excessive lag accumulation.

### Synchronous Replication

PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous by default. If the primary server crashes then some transactions that were committed may not have been replicated to the standby server, causing data loss. The amount of data loss is proportional to the replication delay at the time of failover.

Synchronous replication offers the ability to confirm that all changes made by a transaction have been transferred to one or more synchronous standby servers. This extends that standard level of durability offered by a transaction commit. This level of protection is referred to as 2-safe replication in computer science theory, and group-1-safe (group-safe and 1-safe) when `synchronous_commit` is set to `remote_write`.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:39" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Streaming Replication" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Streaming Replication

Streaming replication is asynchronous by default (see Synchronous Replication), in which case there is a small delay between committing a transaction in the primary and the changes becoming visible in the standby. This delay is however much smaller than with file-based log shipping, typically under one second assuming the standby is powerful enough to keep up with the load. With streaming replication, `archive_timeout` is not required to reduce the data loss window.
</source>

### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

### Caveats

- Valid starting points for standby queries are generated at each checkpoint on the primary. If the standby is shut down while the primary is in a shutdown state, it might not be possible to re-enter hot standby until the primary is started up, so that it generates further starting points in the WAL logs. This situation isn't a problem in the most common situations where it might happen. Generally, if the primary is shut down and not available anymore, that's likely due to a serious failure that requires the standby being converted to operate as the new primary anyway. And in situations where the primary is being intentionally taken down, coordinating to make sure the standby becomes the new primary smoothly is also standard procedure.

To use streaming replication, set up a file-based log-shipping standby server as described in Log-Shipping Standby Servers. Based on the documentation, here's how to measure PostgreSQL standby lag:

## Primary Methods

### 1. **Using `pg_stat_replication` View** (from primary server)

Query the following from your primary database to see which standbys are connected:

```sql
-- View all replica connections with their current LSN positions
SELECT 
    client_addr AS 'Client IP',
    application_name AS 'Application Name',
    sync_state AS 'Sync State',
    sent_lsn AS 'Sent LSN',
    flush_lsn AS 'Flush LSN',
    reply_lsn AS 'Reply LSN'
FROM pg_stat_replication;
```

### 2. **Calculate Replication Lag**

Use these LSN differences to identify bottlenecks:

| Metric | Calculation | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| **Primary→Network delay** | `pg_current_wal_lsn - sent_lsn` | Large values indicate primary is under heavy load |
| **Network→Standby load** | `sent_lsn - pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` | Indicates network delays or heavy standby load |
| **WAL→Replay delay** | `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn - flushed_lsn` | WAL received faster than it can be replayed |

### 3. **Hot Standby Monitoring** (if applicable)

For hot standbys, also query these additional views:

```sql
-- WAL receiver status
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_wal_receiver;

-- Recovery progress
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_recovery;
```

### 4. **Calculate Time-Based Lag**

From the standby side, you can calculate lag in time by comparing WAL positions and multiplying by average throughput. The actual time lag calculation would require knowing the WAL generation rate (bytes/second or transactions per second).

## Key Findings

As noted in the incident INC-2093 ([D11:2]), replication lag can become critical during outages, as seen when a standby fell 38 minutes behind the primary during a registry outage, causing extended failover time.

The documents emphasize setting appropriate delay parameters for production standby servers to prevent excessive lag accumulation.

### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

### Caveats

- Valid starting points for standby queries are generated at each checkpoint on the primary. If the standby is shut down while the primary is in a shutdown state, it might not be possible to re-enter hot standby until the primary is started up, so that it generates further starting points in the WAL logs. This situation isn't a problem in the most common situations where it might happen. Generally, if the primary is shut down and not available anymore, that's likely due to a serious failure that requires the standby being converted to operate as the new primary anyway. And in situations where the primary is being intentionally taken down, coordinating to make sure the standby becomes the new primary smoothly is also standard procedure.
</source>

### Streaming Replication

To use streaming replication, set up a file-based log-shipping standby server as described in Log-Shipping Standby Servers. The step that turns a file-based log-shipping standby into streaming replication standby is setting the `primary_conninfo` setting to point to the primary server. Set section guc-listen-addresses and authentication options (see `pg_hba.conf`) on the primary so that the standby server can connect to the `replication` pseudo-database on the primary server (see Authentication).

On systems that support the keepalive socket option, setting section guc-tcp-keepalives-idle, section guc-tcp-keepalives-interval and section guc-tcp-keepalives-count helps the primary promptly notice a broken connection.
</source>

The data on the standby takes some time to arrive from the primary server so there will be a measurable delay between primary and standby. ### Preparing the Primary for Standby Servers

If you want to use streaming replication, set up authentication on the primary server to allow replication connections from the standby server(s); that is, create a role and provide a suitable entry or entries in `pg_hba.conf` with the database field set to `replication`. Also ensure `max_wal_senders` is set to a sufficiently large value in the configuration file of the primary server. If replication slots will be used, ensure that `max_replication_slots` is set sufficiently high as well.

You can retrieve a list of WAL sender processes via the  pg_stat_replication view. Large differences between `pg_current_wal_lsn` and the view's `sent_lsn` field might indicate that the primary server is under heavy load, while differences between `sent_lsn` and `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` on the standby might indicate network delay, or that the standby is under heavy load.

Based on the documentation, here's how to measure PostgreSQL standby lag:

## Primary Methods

### 1. **Using `pg_stat_replication` View** (from primary server)

Query the following from your primary database to see which standbys are connected:

```sql
-- View all replica connections with their current LSN positions
SELECT 
    client_addr AS 'Client IP',
    application_name AS 'Application Name',
    sync_state AS 'Sync State',
    sent_lsn AS 'Sent LSN',
    flush_lsn AS 'Flush LSN',
    reply_lsn AS 'Reply LSN'
FROM pg_stat_replication;
```

### 2. **Calculate Replication Lag**

Use these LSN differences to identify bottlenecks:

## Key Metrics for Measuring Replication Lag

**From the primary server:**
- **`pg_current_wal_lsn`**: Current Write Location (WAL LSN)

- Primary: `pg_current_wal_lsn`
- Standby: `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn`

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. ### Synchronous Replication

PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous by default. If the primary server crashes then some transactions that were committed may not have been replicated to the standby server, causing data loss. The amount of data loss is proportional to the replication delay at the time of failover.

Synchronous replication offers the ability to confirm that all changes made by a transaction have been transferred to one or more synchronous standby servers. This extends that standard level of durability offered by a transaction commit. This level of protection is referred to as 2-safe replication in computer science theory, and group-1-safe (group-safe and 1-safe) when `synchronous_commit` is set to `remote_write`.
</source>

### Streaming Replication

Streaming replication is asynchronous by default (see Synchronous Replication), in which case there is a small delay between committing a transaction in the primary and the changes becoming visible in the standby. This delay is however much smaller than with file-based log shipping, typically under one second assuming the standby is powerful enough to keep up with the load. With streaming replication, `archive_timeout` is not required to reduce the data loss window.
</source>

Here's how to do it:

**Measure Replication Lag:**
Compare the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby:

| Location | How to Query | Server |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| Current WAL position on primary | `pg_current_wal_lsn()` | Primary server |
| Last WAL received by standby | `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()` | Standby server |

These functions return an LSN (Log Sequence Number) value that indicates progress through the WAL archive.

**Additional Monitoring Options:**
- The last WAL receive location is also visible in the process status of the WAL receiver process (you can see this with the `ps` command).
- You can view this information in the `pg_stat_replication` view for detailed replication metrics.
- In asynchronous replication, there will always be some lag window where changes made on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby [D07:2].

**Example SQL queries:**

```sql
-- On the primary server
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();

-- On the standby server
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
```

You should compare these LSN values - the difference represents the lag amount. A smaller difference indicates better replication health.

## What made it worse

For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:76" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Read-Your-Writes Consistency" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:46" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Streaming Replication > Monitoring" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Monitoring

An important health indicator of streaming replication is the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby. You can calculate this lag by comparing the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby. These locations can be retrieved using `pg_current_wal_lsn` on the primary and `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` on the standby, respectively (see section functions-admin-backup-table and section functions-recovery-info-table for details). The last WAL receive location in the standby is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process, displayed using the `ps` command (see section monitoring-ps for details).
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:73" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for High Availability" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for High Availability

When a standby first attaches to the primary, it will not yet be properly synchronized. This is described as `catchup` mode. Once the lag between standby and primary reaches zero for the first time we move to real-time `streaming` state. The catch-up duration may be long immediately after the standby has been created. If the standby is shut down, then the catch-up period will increase according to the length of time the standby has been down. The standby is only able to become a synchronous standby once it has reached `streaming` state. This state can be viewed using the pg_stat_replication view.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:24" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Data Checksums > Online Enabling of Checksums > Impact on System of Online Operations" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Impact on System of Online Operations

- Replication: When the standby receives the data checksum state change in the WAL stream it will issue a restartpoint in order to flush the current state into the `pg_control` file. The restartpoint will flush the current state to disk and will block redo until finished. This in turn will induce replication lag, which on synchronous standbys also blocks the primary. Reducing section guc-max-wal-size before the process is started can help with reducing the time it takes for the restartpoint to finish.
</source>

answers:
Based on the company's internal Prometheus documentation, **you should use `rate` for alerts**, not `irate`. 

Here's what the documentation states:

> Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are hard to read. [D07:1]

The key differences between the two functions:

- **`rate()`**: Should be used for alerts because it averages over the range vector (e.g., 5m). This reduces noise from brief spikes that might trigger false positives. It works better with slower-moving counters.

- **`irate()`**: Should only be used when graphing "volatile, fast-moving counters" because it calculates the per-second instant rate based on just the last two data points. However, it breaks easily on counter resets and is too noisy for reliable alerting.

**Best practice**: Use `rate` for alert conditions to avoid false positives from transient spikes while still detecting meaningful issues.

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:60" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `irate()`" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## `irate()`

```
irate(http_requests_total{job="api-server"}[5m])
```

`irate` should only be used when graphing volatile, fast-moving counters.
Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes
in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare
spikes are hard to read.

Note that when combining `irate()` with an
aggregation operator (e.g. `sum()`)
or a function aggregating over time (any function ending in `_over_time`),
always take an `irate()` first, then aggregate. Otherwise `irate()` cannot detect
counter resets when your target restarts.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:59" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `irate()`" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## `irate()`

`irate(v range-vector)` calculates the per-second instant rate of increase of
the time series in the range vector. This is based on the last two data points.
Breaks in monotonicity (such as counter resets due to target restarts) are
automatically adjusted for. Both samples must be either float samples or
histogram samples. Elements in `v` where one of the last two samples is a float
sample and the other is a histogram sample will be omitted from the result
vector, flagged by a warn-level annotation.

`irate` should only be used with counters (for both floats and histograms).

The following example expression returns the per-second rate of HTTP requests
looking up to 5 minutes back for the two most recent data points, per time
series in the range vector:
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md:8" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md" title="The Zen of Prometheus" section="The Zen of Prometheus > First the rate, then aggregate" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## First the rate, then aggregate

Be aware of counter resets.
    As stated in Rate then sum, never sum then rate.
    As a rule of thumb, the only mathematical operations you can safely directly apply to a counter's values are `rate`, `irate`, `increase`, and `resets`. Anything else will cause you problems.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/feature_flags.md:15" doc="prometheus-server/feature_flags.md" title="Feature flags" section="Feature flags > Start timestamp (ST) usage in PromQL functions" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Start timestamp (ST) usage in PromQL functions

`--enable-feature=use-start-timestamps`

Enables the use of start timestamps (ST) in PromQL functions such as `rate()`, `irate()`, `increase()` and `start_timestamp()`. This feature doesn't currently work with extended range selectors.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md:8" doc="prometheus-server/configuration/alerting_rules.md" title="Alerting rules" section="Alerting rules > Sending alert notifications" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Sending alert notifications

Prometheus's alerting rules are good at figuring what is broken *right now*, but
they are not a fully-fledged notification solution. Another layer is needed to
add summarization, notification rate limiting, silencing and alert dependencies
on top of the simple alert definitions. In Prometheus's ecosystem, the
Alertmanager takes on this
role. Thus, Prometheus may be configured to periodically send information about
alert states to an Alertmanager instance, which then takes care of dispatching
the right notifications.
Prometheus can be configured to automatically discover available
Alertmanager instances through its service discovery integrations.
</source>

Based on the Prometheus vendor documentation, **you should use `rate` for alerts**.

According to [Prometheus's Query Functions documentation]([prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:60](https://example.com/prometheus-server/querying/functions.md)):

> "`irate` should only be used when graphing volatile, fast-moving counters. Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are hard to read."

**Why use `rate` instead of `irate` for alerts:**

1. **Brief spikes issue**: `irate()` is calculated from only the last two data points (2-second resolution), so brief rate increases could trigger an alert that would immediately resolve again. This "flickering" can waste resources on repetitive notifications.

2. **FOR clause stability**: Brief rate changes with `irate()` can cause your alert duration threshold (`FOR`) clause to reset, leading to unpredictable alert behavior.

3. **Smaller window**: `rate()` uses the full evaluation range (e.g., 5m or 1h), giving you a smoother, more stable representation of trends.

**Summary**:
- **Alerts → Use `rate()`**
- **Graphing volatile/fast-changing metrics → Use `irate()`**

This is the recommended approach in the "Zen of Prometheus" principles for alert monitoring.

**For alerts, use `rate()`** - not `irate()`.

The documentation explicitly states: *"Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are hard to read."* [D07:2]

**When to use each:**
- **`rate()`**: For alerts and slower-moving metrics where you want to smooth out transient noise
- **`irate()`**: For graphing volatile, fast-moving counters where you need immediate detection of rapid increases

The general rule of thumb is: *"First the rate, then aggregate"*—always apply `rate()` or `irate()` first to counters, then sum if needed [D07:4].

You get one notification instead of hundreds because your Alertmanager is configured to **group alerts**.

When many systems fail simultaneously, each failing instance generates its own alert. Without grouping, this would result in hundreds or thousands of separate notifications. However, your Alertmanager automatically consolidates similar alerts into a single notification based on their labels—typically grouping by things like:
- Cluster name
- Alert rule name

This creates "compact" notifications that list all affected service instances in one message rather than sending individual pages for each failure.

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and

cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances

instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.

answers:
You get one notification instead of hundreds because of **Alertmanager's grouping and deduplication features**. Here's how it works:

**1. Grouping:** Alertmanager categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously [D07:2].

**2. Deduplication across Alertmanager instances:** When you have multiple Alertmanager instances running in a high availability setup, they use a gossip mechanism to coordinate. For example:
- AM-1 (position 0): Waits 0 seconds, sends notification, logs to nflog
- AM-2 (position 1): Waits 15 seconds, checks notification log, sees AM-1's entry, **skips** notification
- AM-3 (position 2): Waits 30 seconds, sees AM-1's entry, **skips** notification  
Result: Exactly one notification sent by only one instance [D07:3].

This design ensures you receive meaningful, consolidated updates rather than dozens of identical alarms about the same incident, while still prioritizing getting *at least* one notification over potentially missing an alert entirely.

### Behavior During Partition

**In Partition A** (AM-1 alone):
- AM-1 sees itself as position 0
- Waits 0 × timeout = 0 seconds
- Sends notifications (no dedup from AM-2/AM-3)

**In Partition B** (AM-2, AM-3):
- AM-2 is position 0, AM-3 is position 1
- AM-2 waits 0 seconds, sends notification
- AM-3 sees AM-2's notification log entry, deduplicates

**Result**: Duplicate notifications sent (one from Partition A, one from Partition B)

This is **intentional** - Alertmanager prefers duplicate notifications over missed alerts.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:34" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > How It Works: End-to-End Example > Scenario: 3-instance cluster, new alert group" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Scenario: 3-instance cluster, new alert group

1. **Alert arrives** at all 3 instances from Prometheus
2. **Dispatcher** creates aggregation group, waits `group_wait` (e.g., 30s)
3. **After group_wait**:
   - Each instance prepares to notify
4. **Notifier stage**:
   - All instances wait for gossip to settle (if just started)
   - **AM-1** (position 0): waits 0s, checks notification log (empty), sends notification, logs to nflog
   - **AM-2** (position 1): waits 15s, checks notification log (sees AM-1's entry), **skips** notification
   - **AM-3** (position 2): waits 30s, checks notification log (sees AM-1's entry), **skips** notification
5. **Result**: Exactly one notification sent (by AM-1)
</source>

The notifications sent to receivers are constructed via templates. The Alertmanager comes with default templates but they can also be customized.
To avoid confusion it's important to note that the Alertmanager templates differ from templating in Prometheus, however Prometheus templating also includes the templating in alert rule labels/annotations.

The Alertmanager's notification templates are based on the Go templating system.
Note that some fields are evaluated as text, and others as HTML which will affect escaping.
</source>

### Behavior During Partition

**In Partition A** (AM-1 alone):
- AM-1 sees itself as position 0
- Waits 0 × timeout = 0 seconds
- Sends notifications (no dedup from AM-2/AM-3)

**In Partition B** (AM-2, AM-3):
- AM-2 is position 0, AM-3 is position 1
- AM-2 waits 0 seconds, sends notification
- AM-3 sees AM-2's notification log entry, deduplicates

**Result**: Duplicate notifications sent (one from Partition A, one from Partition B)

This is **intentional** - Alertmanager prefers duplicate notifications over missed alerts.
</source>

### Scenario: 3-instance cluster, new alert group

1. **Alert arrives** at all 3 instances from Prometheus
2. **Dispatcher** creates aggregation group, waits `group_wait` (e.g., 30s)
3. **After group_wait**:
   - Each instance prepares to notify
4. **Notifier stage**:
   - All instances wait for gossip to settle (if just started)
   - **AM-1** (position 0): waits 0s, checks notification log (empty), sends notification, logs to nflog
   - **AM-2** (position 1): waits 15s, checks notification log (sees AM-1's entry), **skips** notification
   - **AM-3** (position 2): waits 30s, checks notification log (sees AM-1's entry), **skips** notification
5. **Result**: Exactly one notification sent (by AM-1)
</source>

### Prometheus Configuration

**Important**: Configure Prometheus to send alerts to **all** Alertmanager instances, not via a load balancer.

```yaml
# prometheus.yml
alerting:

    - static_configs:
        - targets:
            - am-1.example.com:9093
            - am-2.example.com:9093
            - am-3.example.com:9093

#### 3. Deduplication via Notification Log

The `DedupStage` queries the notification log to determine if a notification should be sent:

```go
// Check notification log for recent sends
entry := nflog.Query(receiver, groupKey)
if entry.exists && !shouldNotify(entry, alerts, repeatInterval) {
    // Skip: already notified recently
    return nil
}
```

Deduplication checks:
- **Firing alerts changed?** If yes, notify
- **Resolved alerts changed?** If yes and `send_resolved: true`, notify
- **Repeat interval elapsed?** If yes, notify
- **Otherwise**: Skip notification (deduplicated)

The notification log is replicated via gossip, so all cluster members share the same send history.
</source>

### Debug duplicate notifications

Duplicate notifications can occur due to:

1. **Network partitions** (expected, fail-open)
2. **Gossip not settled** - Check `--cluster.settle-timeout`
3. **Clock skew** - Ensure NTP is configured on all instances
4. **Notification log not replicating** - Check gossip metrics

Enable debug logging:

```bash
alertmanager --log.level=debug
```

Look for:
- `"Waiting for gossip to settle..."`
- `"gossip settled; proceeding"`
- Deduplication decisions in notification pipeline
</source>

answers:
Based on the company's alerting system using **Alertmanager**, you receive only one notification instead of hundreds due to **inhibition** — a built-in feature designed exactly to prevent notification storms during mass failures.

## How Inhibition Works

When multiple systems fail at once, your Alertmanager is configured with inhibition rules that allow it to suppress notifications for related alerts once a broader incident alert has fired. This prevents you from being overwhelmed with hundreds of duplicate or redundant notifications.

### Example Scenario

Imagine 100 individual database servers all go down simultaneously. Without inhibition, you'd receive 100 separate alerts. However, your Alertmanager likely has a rule like:

- **Source Alert:** A cluster-level or region-level service unavailable alert fires first
- **Target Alerts:** All 100 individual server alerts
- **Inhibition Rule:** When the source alert is firing, mute (suppress) all matching target alerts

The result: You get one consolidated notification about the cluster issue, not 100 individual ones.

## Inhibition Rules Configuration

These rules are configured in the Alertmanager configuration file and work as follows:

```yaml
# Each alert is either a "source" or "target"
inhibit_rules:
  - name: 'supress related alerts'
    # Source alert (what triggers suppression):
    source_matchers:
      [ - severity=critical ]
    
    # Target alert (what gets silenced):
    target_matchers:
      [ - severity=warning ]
    
    # Both must share these label values:
    equal:
      [ - alertname, namespace ]
```

This ensures that if a critical cluster alert fires, all related but less severe alerts won't trigger additional notifications.

## Other Alertmanager Features

Your notification count is also controlled by other mechanisms:
- **Aggregation/Grouping**: Related alerts are grouped together so they're sent in batches rather than one-by-one
- **Silencing**: You can manually silence specific alert combinations while troubleshooting
- **Repeat Interval**: Controls how often repeated notifications are sent (default: no repeats unless new alerts fire)

So you're not missing information — the system is intentionally consolidating alerts to focus on the actual issues rather than flooding you with noise from correlated failures.

## Inhibition

Inhibition is a concept of suppressing notifications for certain alerts if
certain other alerts are already firing.

**Example:** An alert is firing that informs that an entire cluster is not
reachable. Alertmanager can be configured to mute all other alerts concerning
this cluster if that particular alert is firing.
This prevents notifications for hundreds or thousands of firing alerts that
are unrelated to the actual issue.

Inhibitions are configured through the Alertmanager's configuration file.
</source>

Based on the company's alerting system using **Alertmanager**, you receive only one notification instead of hundreds due to **inhibition** — a built-in feature designed exactly to prevent notification storms during mass failures.

## How Inhibition Works

When multiple systems fail at once, your Alertmanager is configured with inhibition rules that allow it to suppress notifications for related alerts once a broader incident alert has fired. This prevents you from being overwhelmed with hundreds of duplicate or redundant notifications.

### Example Scenario

Imagine 100 individual database servers all go down simultaneously. Without inhibition, you'd receive 100 separate alerts. However, your Alertmanager likely has a rule like:

- **Source Alert:** A cluster-level or region-level service unavailable alert fires first
- **Target Alerts:** All 100 individual server alerts
- **Inhibition Rule:** When the source alert is firing, mute (suppress) all matching target alerts

The result: You get one consolidated notification about the cluster issue, not 100 individual ones.

## Inhibition Rules Configuration

These rules are configured in the Alertmanager configuration file and work as follows:

```yaml
# Each alert is either a "source" or "target"
inhibit_rules:
  - name: 'supress related alerts'
    # Source alert (what triggers suppression):
    source_matchers:
      [ - severity=critical ]
    
    # Target alert (what gets silenced):
    target_matchers:
      [ - severity=warning ]
    
    # Both must share these label values:
    equal:
      [ - alertname, namespace ]
```

This ensures that if a critical cluster alert fires, all related but less severe alerts won't trigger additional notifications.

## Other Alertmanager Features

Your notification count is also controlled by other mechanisms:
- **Aggregation/Grouping**: Related alerts are grouped together so they're sent in batches rather than one-by-one
- **Silencing**: You can manually silence specific alert combinations while troubleshooting
- **Repeat Interval**: Controls how often repeated notifications are sent (default: no repeats unless new alerts fire)

So you're not missing information — the system is intentionally consolidating alerts to focus on the actual issues rather than flooding you with noise from correlated failures.

You get only one notification instead of hundreds because **Alertmanager uses deduplication** to prevent notification storms. Here's how it works:

## How Deduplication Works

### 1. **Group-Based Aggregation**
When multiple systems fail simultaneously, their alerts are grouped together and processed as a single alert group rather than sending individual notifications for each failure [D097:15].

### 2. **Notification Log Deduplication**
Each Alertmanager instance maintains a notification log (`nflog`) that tracks who has been notified. Before sending a notification, the system checks:
- **Firing alerts changed?** If yes, notify
- **Resolved alerts changed?** If yes and configured to send resolved alerts, notify  
- **Repeat interval elapsed?** If yes, notify
- **Otherwise**: Skip notification (deduplicated) [D097:15]

### 3. **High Availability Gossip-Based Deduplication**
In a clustered environment (multiple Alertmanager instances), the notification log is replicated via gossip, so all instances share the same send history. This prevents duplicates across instances [D097:13].

### 4. **Position-Based Staggered Waits**
To further ensure consistency, Alertmanager instances wait based on their alphabetical position in the peer list:
- First instance (position 0): sends immediately after checking
- Second instance (position 1): waits longer, then checks log
- Third instance (position 2): waits even longer...
This staggered timing allows the first instance to write to the log before others check [D097:13].

**Example**: With 3 instances in a cluster and a 15-second peer timeout:
- AM-1 sends at t=0
- AM-2 tries to send but sees AM-1's entry in the log → skips
- AM-3 also sees AM-1's entry → skips
- **Result**: Exactly one notification sent total [D097:9].

This approach ensures you receive exactly one comprehensive notification about multiple failures without overwhelming your communication channels.

Based on the registry documentation, **it's generally not OK** for two services to share one registry key. Here's why:

## Rate Limiting Issues

According to the Registry API reference [D01:8], **each key has rate limits** (60 requests per minute), and **"two processes sharing one key share one limit."** 

From the Agent owners' FAQ [D14:3]:

> "If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key."

This creates several problems:

- **Competing for limited requests**: If Service A needs 30 requests/minute and Service B needs 20 requests/minute, but they share a key with only 60 request/minute limit, either service could get throttled.
- **Performance impact**: When rate-limited, services receive HTTP 429 errors with `Retry-After` headers, causing unexpected latency [D05:4].
- **Resource contention**: Even without hitting the hard limit, sharing the key can lead to inefficient use of quota as documented in [D08:4].

## Best Practice

Your registry should assign **one dedicated key per service/process**. Each service gets its own read-write or read-only key, avoiding conflicts and ensuring predictable performance.

## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D08:4" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Polling the registry from your own dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Polling the registry from your own dashboards

If you build your own dashboard on top of the registry, poll no more than once every few seconds. The registry allows 100 requests per minute per key, and a dashboard that uses most of that leaves nothing for the agent sharing its key.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.

### Rate Limit Sharing
According to the Registry API reference [D01:8], each key has rate limits of **60 requests per minute**, and **"limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit."**

- Production agents and monitoring dashboards
- Multiple applications or microservices
- Different tiers or ownership domains

This prevents resource contention and ensures each service gets predictable access to the registry without interference from other processes sharing the same key.

## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.

<source id="D05:4" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 4: Check for rate limiting" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 4: Check for rate limiting

Look for `REG-1009` responses in the agent's logs. An agent that's being rate-limited waits for `Retry-After` on every call, which looks like latency. If you find them, check whether another process is sharing the agent's key.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D08:4" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Polling the registry from your own dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Polling the registry from your own dashboards

If you build your own dashboard on top of the registry, poll no more than once every few seconds. The registry allows 100 requests per minute per key, and a dashboard that uses most of that leaves nothing for the agent sharing its key.
</source>

<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent <agent_name> --scope <read|write>
```

**Example:**

regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

- You'll need to revoke the old key within 24 hours of issuing the new one

content.content:
<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |
| `REG-1004` | `FORBIDDEN_FIELD` | 403 | The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key. |
</source>

Based on the documentation, here's where slowdowns typically come from during agent latency investigations:

**Most Common Sources:**

1. **Rate Limiting (REG-1009)** - This is a primary culprit. When agents are rate-limited, they wait for `Retry-After` headers on every call, which appears as significant latency [D05:4][D02:2]. Each key gets 60 requests per minute, and multiple processes sharing one key compete for the same limit [D01:8].

## Asynchronous Commit

Asynchronous commit provides behavior different from setting section guc-fsync = off. `fsync` is a server-wide setting that will alter the behavior of all transactions. It disables all logic within PostgreSQL that attempts to synchronize writes to different portions of the database, and therefore a system crash (that is, a hardware or operating system crash, not a failure of PostgreSQL itself) could result in arbitrarily bad corruption of the database state. is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

**Example:** Dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your
cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances
can no longer reach the database.
Alerting rules in Prometheus were configured to send an alert for each service
instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.

Based on the company's documentation, here's where agent latency slowdowns usually come from:

## Primary Sources of Latency

### 1. **Tool/Backend Service Slowdowns** [D05:2]
> "Most spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model."

This is the most common cause. When an agent needs to call external services or tools, those backends can become slow or unresponsive, causing delays that appear as increased p95 response times.

### 2. **Rate Limiting** [D05:4] [D01:8] [D03:2]
Agents can be rate-limited by the Registry API, resulting in HTTP 429 responses with `REG-1009` error codes and `Retry-After` headers. When rate-limited, agents must wait for the specified retry time on every call, which creates apparent latency. This often happens when multiple processes share the same agent key and exceed the 60 requests per minute limit per key.

### 3. **Registry Service Issues** [D02:3]
Problems with the Registry API itself, including:
- `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` - Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row
- General slow response from the registry service

### 4. **Heavy Polling from Dashboards** [D03:2]
Internal dashboards can sometimes poll aggressively enough to slow the registry for other agents (this was fixed in v2.4).

---

**Investigation approach:** According to the runbook, you should confirm the issue on the dashboard, then open slow sessions to identify which specific tool call is timing out (most often one tool rather than the model itself) before escalating to the owning team or Platform [D05:2][D05:5].

## Primary Sources of Latency

### 1. **Tool/Backend Service Slowdowns** [D05:2]
> "Most spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model."

Based on the company's documentation and runbooks, here's where slowdowns in agent latency investigations typically come from:

## Primary Source: Slow Tool Calls

According to the [agent latency spike runbook](D05:1), **most latency spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model**. The investigation process involves:

1. **Confirming the spike is real** by checking the dashboard and p95 response times
2. **Finding the slow step** by examining recent slow sessions and looking at time spent in each tool call vs model call
3. **Escalating to the owning team** once the slow service/tool is identified

## Common Causes

Based on the documentation, the typical sources are:

| Cause | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Slow external services** | One of the tools the agent calls gets slow or unresponsive |
| **Rate limiting** | Responses like `REG-1009` cause the agent to wait for `Retry-After` headers on every call |
| **Database bottlenecks** | PostgreSQL connection pool exhaustion or query slowness affecting tool calls |
| **Network issues** | Connectivity problems between the agent and its services |

As noted in the alerting practices documentation, you should "alert on high latency... as high up in the stack as possible" and focus on user-visible latency rather than lower-level component issues unless they're causing direct impact.

The key insight from the runbook is that **the agent's model is rarely the culprit** - you'll almost always find a specific tool or downstream service that's the bottleneck.

## When does it fit?

Prometheus works well for recording any purely numeric time series. It fits
both machine-centric monitoring as well as monitoring of highly dynamic
service-oriented architectures. In a world of microservices, its support for
multi-dimensional data collection and querying is a particular strength.

Prometheus is designed for reliability, to be the system you go to
during an outage to allow you to quickly diagnose problems. Each Prometheus
server is standalone, not depending on network storage or other remote services.
You can rely on it when other parts of your infrastructure are broken, and
you do not need to set up extensive infrastructure to use it.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:23" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

Directly moving WAL records from one database server to another is typically described as log shipping. PostgreSQL implements file-based log shipping by transferring WAL records one file (WAL segment) at a time. WAL files (16MB) can be shipped easily and cheaply over any distance, whether it be to an adjacent system, another system at the same site, or another system on the far side of the globe. The bandwidth required for this technique varies according to the transaction rate of the primary server. Record-based log shipping is more granular and streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection (see Streaming Replication).
</source>

#### Libraries

Libraries should provide instrumentation with no additional configuration
required by users.

If it is a library used to access some resource outside of the process (for example,
network, disk, or IPC), track the overall query count, errors (if errors are possible)
and latency at a minimum.

Depending on how heavy the library is, track internal errors and
latency within the library itself, and any general statistics you think may be
useful.

A library may be used by multiple independent parts of an application against
different resources, so take care to distinguish uses with labels where
appropriate. For example, a database connection pool should distinguish the databases
it is talking to, whereas there is no need to differentiate
between users of a DNS client library.
</source>

### User's Overview

During hot standby, the parameter `transaction_read_only` is always true and may not be changed. But as long as no attempt is made to modify the database, connections during hot standby will act much like any other database connection. If failover or switchover occurs, the database will switch to normal processing mode. Sessions will remain connected while the server changes mode. Once hot standby finishes, it will be possible to initiate read-write transactions (even from a session begun during hot standby).
</source>

## Delay compaction start time

`--enable-feature=delayed-compaction`

A random offset, up to `10%` of the chunk range, is added to the Head compaction start time. This assists Prometheus instances in avoiding simultaneous compactions and reduces the load on shared resources.

Only auto Head compactions and the operations directly resulting from them are subject to this delay.

In the event of multiple consecutive Head compactions being possible, only the first compaction experiences this delay.

Note that during this delay, the Head continues its usual operations, which include serving and appending series.

Despite the delay in compaction, the blocks produced are time-aligned in the same manner as they would be if the delay was not in place.
</source>

### Handling Query Conflicts

When a conflicting query is short, it's typically desirable to allow it to complete by delaying WAL application for a little bit; but a long delay in WAL application is usually not desirable. So the cancel mechanism has parameters, section guc-max-standby-archive-delay and section guc-max-standby-streaming-delay, that define the maximum allowed delay in WAL application. Conflicting queries will be canceled once it has taken longer than the relevant delay setting to apply any newly-received WAL data. There are two parameters so that different delay values can be specified for the case of reading WAL data from an archive (i.e., initial recovery from a base backup or “catching up” a standby server that has fallen far behind) versus reading WAL data via streamin
</source>
